session.question: How textile waste management can use waste conversion and the adsorption properties in these materials?
session.answer:
Textile waste management can adopt a waste-to-adsorbent strategy by converting discarded fibers, fabrics, and related biowaste into biochar, activated carbon, carbonized fibers, or cellulose-based sorbents. These materials can be engineered through feedstock selection, pyrolysis/carbonization, and physical, chemical, or biological modification to increase surface area, porosity, and functional groups, thereby improving contaminant uptake. (laishram2025advancementsinbiochar chunk 1, jha2023biocharassustainable chunk 1)

The adsorption properties of these converted materials are particularly useful for treating textile wastewater, where dyes, metals, and other pollutants are major targets. Biochar-based adsorbents show high efficiencies for heavy metals such as lead and cadmium, as well as organic pollutants including dyes and phenols, while also contributing to microplastic and nanoplastic reduction. Mesoporous activated carbon derived from biomass demonstrates the same concept at high performance, with a BET surface area of 480 m2/g, mesopores around 4 nm, strong adsorption of hazardous dyes, and Langmuir/pseudo-second-order behavior consistent with monolayer chemisorption. (laishram2025advancementsinbiochar chunk 1, reddy2024biomassderivedsustainablemesoporous chunk 1)

Mechanistically, pollutant removal occurs through π-π interactions, hydrogen bonding, electrostatic attraction, and chemisorption on porous carbon frameworks with graphitic character. Reusability is also important: regenerated adsorbents can be reused over multiple cycles, which supports sustainable textile waste management and lowers disposal burden. (reddy2024biomassderivedsustainablemesoporous chunk 1, jha2023biocharassustainable chunk 1)

A circular implementation is to integrate textile waste valorization, adsorption-based treatment, and regeneration/recovery steps, so that waste is first converted into an adsorbent, then used to remove pollutants from wastewater, and finally reused or further converted into energy or additional carbon products. (kalengyo2023utilizingorangepeel chunk 1, jha2023biocharassustainable chunk 1)

pqac-5b6fdf0f: The excerpt is a review on biochar as a sustainable adsorbent for water pollution mitigation. It explains that biochar is a carbon-rich material made from biomass wastes and can be engineered through feedstock selection, pyrolysis/carbonization and physical, chemical, or biological modification to improve contaminant removal. The review highlights high removal efficiencies for heavy metals like lead and cadmium, and strong adsorption of organic pollutants such as dyes and phenols, plus reductions in microplastics/nanoplastics. It also discusses related preparation technologies and pollutant-removal mechanisms, which is relevant to converting textile waste into adsorbents such as biochar, activated carbon, carbonized fibers, or cellulose-based sorbents for dye, metal, and pollutant removal.
From Devika Laishram, S. N. Kim, Seul‐Yi Lee, and Soo‐Jin Park. Advancements in biochar as a sustainable adsorbent for water pollution mitigation. Advanced Science, 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.202410383, doi:10.1002/advs.202410383.

pqac-4b6d8efd: The excerpt describes a biomass-derived mesoporous activated carbon (MAC) made from Ficus religiosa leaves and used to adsorb hazardous dyes from wastewater, showing how waste biomass can be converted into a high-surface-area adsorbent. The material had a surface area of 480 m2/g and mesopores around 4 nm, with strong adsorption performance for acid blue 9 and malachite green. Adsorption followed Langmuir isotherm behavior and pseudo-second-order kinetics, indicating monolayer chemisorption. The work highlights sustainability, low cost, and recyclability over five adsorption-desorption cycles. This supports the broader idea of converting waste textiles or biomass into biochar, activated carbon, carbonized fibers, or cellulose-based sorbents for removing dyes and other pollutants from wastewater.
From Y. Subba Reddy, Naresh Kumar Rotte, B.K. Sudhakar, Navin Chand, Ramavath Janraj Naik, Sudip Mandal, and M. Ravi Chandra. Biomass-derived sustainable mesoporous activated carbon as an efficient and recyclable adsorbent for the adsorption of hazardous dyes. Hybrid Advances, 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.hybadv.2024.100218, doi:10.1016/j.hybadv.2024.100218.

pqac-69925682: The excerpt describes a biomass-derived mesoporous activated carbon (MAC) used for wastewater treatment, which is relevant as an example of sustainable adsorption materials. It reports a high BET surface area of 480 m2/g and mesopores around 4 nm, with characterization by FTIR, Raman, SEM/TEM, and other methods confirming a graphitic porous framework. The adsorbent removed hazardous dyes acid blue 9 and malachite green, with adsorption fitting the Langmuir isotherm (monolayer coverage) and pseudo-second-order kinetics, suggesting chemisorption. The proposed mechanisms include π-π interactions, hydrogen bonding, and electrostatic interactions. The material was recyclable for five adsorption-desorption cycles, indicating regeneration and reuse potential.
From Y. Subba Reddy, Naresh Kumar Rotte, B.K. Sudhakar, Navin Chand, Ramavath Janraj Naik, Sudip Mandal, and M. Ravi Chandra. Biomass-derived sustainable mesoporous activated carbon as an efficient and recyclable adsorbent for the adsorption of hazardous dyes. Hybrid Advances, 2024. It highlights that biochar can be produced from waste, and its adsorption performance can be improved by modifying properties such as porosity, surface area, surface charge, and functional groups. The review emphasizes applications in removing pollutants from wastewater and notes regeneration and reuse as important aspects. Although the excerpt does not specifically mention textile waste, the same waste-to-adsorbent concept is relevant for converting textile waste into biochar, activated carbon, carbonized fibers, or cellulose-based sorbents for dye, metal, and pollutant removal.

pqac-08324891: The excerpt describes orange peel biomass used as an adsorbent for textile wastewater treatment, then regenerated and reused for energy recovery. An adsorbent was prepared by mixing orange peel powder with biochar (1:1 w/w) and used to remove COD, TDS, turbidity, and color from textile wastewater within 30 minutes. After adsorption, the spent adsorbent was cleaned and co-digested with cow dung to produce biogas, and the resulting digestate was pyrolyzed to biochar. The system is presented as a waste-to-wealth, circular approach, but the excerpt does not mention specific surface area or functional groups.
From Roice Bwambale Kalengyo, Mona G. Ibrahim, Manabu Fujii, and Mahmoud Nasr. Utilizing orange peel waste biomass in textile wastewater treatment and its recyclability for dual biogas and biochar production: a techno-economic sustainable approach. Biomass Conversion and Biorefinery, 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s13399-023-04111-1, doi:10.1007/s13399-023-04111-1.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a study on converting agro-waste (areca catechu husk) into biochar for textile wastewater treatment, which is relevant as an example of waste-to-adsorbent valorisation. The biochar was produced by low-rate pyrolysis and characterized as having hydroxyl, carboxyl, acid, and ester groups plus a distorted graphite-like carbon structure. SEM showed non-uniform pores and crosslinked pore tunnels that supported physisorption. It removed cationic Rhodamine B and anionic Alizarine red S efficiently (89% and 87% in 40 min), followed pseudo-first-order kinetics, and fit the Langmuir isotherm with capacities of 105.43 and 109.52 mg/g. This supports using converted waste materials as adsorbents for dye removal.
contexts.question: How can textile waste management use waste conversion and the adsorption properties of these materials? Focus on converting textile waste into adsorbents (biochar, activated carbon, carbonized fibers, cellulose-based sorbents) and their use for dye, metal, and pollutant removal.

It highlights that such waste-derived carbon materials can be reduced, reused, and recycled, and are useful for removing refractory pollutants including dyes, heavy metals, pesticides, pharmaceuticals, and PAHs from wastewater. Although the paper focuses on agrowaste rather than textile waste, the main relevance is the general concept of waste-to-adsorbent conversion for pollutant removal, which can be analogously applied to textile waste converted into biochar, activated carbon, or carbonized sorbents.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes pomegranate-peel waste converted into one-step alkaline carbonate activated carbons, emphasizing sustainable waste-to-adsorbent conversion. The resulting materials had very high carbon content (>94%), low ash (1.0%), strong microporosity (>82% micropore volume), high BET surface area , and strong CO2 adsorption capacity (up to 717 mg/g at 3 MPa and 25 °C). Although the paper focuses on gas adsorption rather than textile waste, it is relevant as an example of converting lignocellulosic waste into high-surface-area adsorbents. Such waste-derived carbons could conceptually inform textile waste management by turning waste biomass/textiles into biochar, activated carbon, carbonized fibers, or cellulose-based sorbents for pollutant capture.
contexts.question: How can textile waste management use waste conversion and the adsorption properties of these materials? Focus on converting textile waste into adsorbents (biochar, activated carbon, carbonized fibers, cellulose-based sorbents) and their use for dye, metal, and pollutant removal.

session.formatted_answer:
Question: How textile waste management can use waste conversion and the adsorption properties in these materials?

Textile waste management can adopt a waste-to-adsorbent strategy by converting discarded fibers, fabrics, and related biowaste into biochar, activated carbon, carbonized fibers, or cellulose-based sorbents. These materials can be engineered through feedstock selection, pyrolysis/carbonization, and physical, chemical, or biological modification to increase surface area, porosity, and functional groups, thereby improving contaminant uptake. (laishram2025advancementsinbiochar chunk 1, jha2023biocharassustainable chunk 1)

The adsorption properties of these converted materials are particularly useful for treating textile wastewater, where dyes, metals, and other pollutants are major targets. Biochar-based adsorbents show high efficiencies for heavy metals such as lead and cadmium, as well as organic pollutants including dyes and phenols, while also contributing to microplastic and nanoplastic reduction. Mesoporous activated carbon derived from biomass demonstrates the same concept at high performance, with a BET surface area of 480 m2/g, mesopores around 4 nm, strong adsorption of hazardous dyes, and Langmuir/pseudo-second-order behavior consistent with monolayer chemisorption. (laishram2025advancementsinbiochar chunk 1, reddy2024biomassderivedsustainablemesoporous chunk 1)

Mechanistically, pollutant removal occurs through π-π interactions, hydrogen bonding, electrostatic attraction, and chemisorption on porous carbon frameworks with graphitic character. Reusability is also important: regenerated adsorbents can be reused over multiple cycles, which supports sustainable textile waste management and lowers disposal burden. (reddy2024biomassderivedsustainablemesoporous chunk 1, jha2023biocharassustainable chunk 1)

A circular implementation is to integrate textile waste valorization, adsorption-based treatment, and regeneration/recovery steps, so that waste is first converted into an adsorbent, then used to remove pollutants from wastewater, and finally reused or further converted into energy or additional carbon products. (kalengyo2023utilizingorangepeel chunk 1, jha2023biocharassustainable chunk 1)
